g.passage: Lagos traffic had finally thinned, and the night bus rattled along the expressway with its windows half open. Babatunde, a park ranger heading home from a conference, had given up his seat to Ahanu, a hiker who had missed the last shuttle from the forest reserve and looked as if he had walked the whole way. For twenty minutes they argued about whether the driver should stop for a woman waving at the roadside. Ahanu insisted it was dangerous; Babatunde called him timid. Then Ahanu said, quietly, that he had lost his trail map that morning and spent four hours believing no one would find him. Babatunde stopped talking. He looked at the dark shapes of palms sliding past and, after a while, offered the hiker half of the bread in his bag. Neither mentioned the woman again.

g.passage: Smelling of rosin and damp wood, the music room in Chiang Mai was empty except for Lan, who sat at the piano refusing to play. Ottilie, the old fishmonger who delivered to the school kitchen on Thursdays, had come in to fetch his crate and found the boy there. Two weeks earlier Lan had accused him, loudly and in front of classmates, of cheating his mother on the weight of a catfish. Ottilie had said nothing then. Now he set down the crate and asked whether the piano was broken. Lan shrugged. The old man pressed a single key, then another, finding a children's song with two clumsy fingers. Lan winced, then laughed despite himself, and slid over on the bench. They played it badly together while the rain thickened on the windows, and the scale near the door went on rusting.
g.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone that occurs in the passage?
options: It shifts from playful teasing between friends to bitter resentment over a past accusation.
It shifts from nostalgic memories of the school to anxiety about the approaching storm.
It shifts from formal politeness during the delivery to impatience with an untalented pupil.
It shifts from strained wariness after a quarrel to a hesitant, gentle reconciliation.

seed.conflict: over silence kept to protect someone
seed.topicSeed: a hillside terrace in Busan; an interpreter and her client over silence kept to protect someone

g.passage:
What do I carry, Eunseo asks, when I carry your words?
On the terrace above Busan the laundry snaps like flags,
and Minjun's sentences arrive heavy, one by one,
for me to turn into another tongue.
I trimmed them all week: a name left out,
a date blurred, a brother's debt unspoken,
because the man across the table would have used it.
I called it accuracy. I called it craft.
But tonight, the harbor lights stitching the dark,
I see that what I kept from him was a shelter,
not a mistake, a roof I raised in silence
over someone neither of us will name.
Let the wind take the shirts. I will hold this.
g.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone that occurs in the poem?
options: The speaker moves from calling her omissions craft to seeing them as protection.
The speaker moves from pride in her translation to shame at having deceived her client.
The speaker moves from admiration of the harbor view to irritation with the noisy laundry.
The speaker moves from confusion about her client's language to confidence in her fluency.

g.passage: Folding chairs clattered as I stacked them along the wall of the gymnasium, where our community supper was held each month on the Navajo plateau. I was sixteen and in charge of the fry bread, and my aunt Katerina was in charge of me. All evening she corrected my dough, my oil, my posture. I resented her and said so. Our friend Defne was in the hospital in Gallup, and I wanted to tell her the doctors had stopped talking about next spring. Katerina said no, sharply, and I called her cold. Later, scrubbing the last pan, I noticed her hands shaking. She told me she had once kept the truth from her own sister and never stopped wondering if it had been a kindness. I put the pan down. For the first time I asked her what she would do, and I waited.
g.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone that occurs in the passage?
options: It shifts from excitement about the supper to disappointment that few guests attended.
It shifts from defiant irritation toward the aunt to a more humble, attentive openness.
It shifts from confident certainty about the friend's illness to complete despair about it.
It shifts from affectionate teasing of the aunt to formal respect for her cooking skill.

g.passage: Years later, Nadeesha would still remember the brass tuning fork Hassan carried through the ferry terminal in Colombo that morning. It had belonged to their music teacher, who had died in the spring and left it, by some clerical error, to Hassan rather than to her, the student who had practiced beside him every afternoon. Hassan was the teacher's nephew and could not sing a note. Nadeesha had stopped speaking to him in protest. Now they waited for the same boat, and she watched him turn the fork over in his hands as gulls circled the loading ramp. He struck it once against the bench. A clear tone rose above the engines, and several passengers looked up. Hassan held it out to her without a word. She did not take it yet, but she leaned close enough to hear the note fade.

options: It describes a crowded terminal in detail and then explains why the ferry departs late.

It explains the source of a grudge and then shows a moment that begins to ease it.

g.passage: By the third hour of the wedding in Cairo, the hall was so crowded that Adaeze had to stand on a chair to find her husband's brother. The twins, Edith liked to say, had always been one person split down the middle, and now they were splitting their late father's house as well. Everyone knew the elder twin had won the house in the family's chess match last winter. Edith did not know, until she overheard it near the dessert table, that he had won only because his twin had deliberately lost. Adaeze watched the two men dance with their arms around each other's shoulders, and she began to see the generous move behind the defeat. She climbed down from the chair. On the table, someone had left a cake knife resting across an untouched slice.
g.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the passage?

g.passage: I had been Gopal's apprentice in the bookbinding workshop in Dhaka for only a year when we were hired to empty a widow's house. My name is Efua, and I was restless then; I wanted to sort everything into piles and be done by noon. Gopal moved slowly, opening each ledger and letter as if it might speak. By evening only one item remained: a ragged prayer book with its spine split in three places. I offered to throw it on the cart. __Gopal instead wrapped it in cloth and set it on his own workbench, where it stayed untouched for a week.__ When he finally began repairing it, he let me hold the thread, and I learned that some work cannot be hurried without being lost. Later the widow's grandson came to collect it, and paid in mangoes.

Ruoxi always said no. __That spring, a company offered to buy the counter and the lease for more money than she had earned in a decade.__ She kept the letter folded under the cash box for a month. Valentina, still waiting for her cousin's reply, began bringing her coffee and staying through the evening rush, talking about the buses she would take once the letter came. g.passage: When I first met Tyrese, he was kneeling beside the dry fountain in a courtyard in Port of Spain, clearing leaves from a basin that had not held water in years. I had just bought the house, and I was there to plan where my mother's bed would go when she moved in from the country. Cecile, I kept telling myself, would hate the city. __Tyrese told me his own father had refused to leave his hillside until the day he could no longer climb it.__ He did not say whether that had been wise. I spent the afternoon measuring doorways and thinking less about furniture than about what my mother would lose, and what she might insist on keeping. By evening I had decided to ask her rather than tell her. Tyrese turned on the hose, and the fountain coughed rust.

g.passage: Glasgow rain had pooled on the lid of the rooftop water tank where Saoirse and I used to rehearse, back when we shared a stage at a cabaret on Sauchiehall Street. I climbed up there again last winter to scatter nothing in particular, just to look. Saoirse's mother had made a lamb stew for the cast every opening night, and she never wrote the recipe down. g.passage: "Leave the dough, Leopoldina, it knows what to do," Wolfram said, though I had stopped being his pupil thirty years ago. g.passage: Two rules held in the rented farmhouse in Galway that summer: no one read the letters alone, and no one read them after dark. Orla made the rules, and her brother kept them, mostly because he could not think of better ones. Their mother had written forty-three letters during the year she worked abroad, and the siblings opened one each evening at the kitchen table. Orla read aloud. Her brother listened and said little, because he had failed his driving test that afternoon and could not bring himself to admit it. Orla noticed his silence and did not ask; she only slowed down at the parts where their mother wrote about learning, late in life, to drive. Imani, the neighbor's girl, brought eggs at seven. Orla thanked her and set the basket on the windowsill beside the unopened envelopes.

The narrator criticizes her for ignoring her brother's distress.

g.passage:
Hollis winds the shop clocks every Thursday,
a chore he once lost to Birdie on a bet
in the Manchester chess club, forty years back.
He still says she cheated. She still says
he moved his bishop like a man asleep.
Now she sits on the stool by the regulator
and calls out which ones run slow,
and he turns each key with the care
of someone tightening a promise.
I watch them from the counter, their quarrel
worn smooth as a pocket watch's case,
and think how a debt can turn into a vow.
Outside, the tram bells keep their own time.
g.question: Which choice best describes the speaker's attitude toward Hollis and Birdie?
options: The speaker regards their old rivalry with fondness for the bond it has become.
The speaker views their quarrel with weary impatience because it has never been settled.
The speaker treats their ritual with detached curiosity about how antique clocks are maintained.

g.explanation: 화자는 두 사람의 다툼을 '주머니시계 케이스처럼 닳아 매끄러워진' 것으로 묘사해 오랜 경쟁이 친숙한 것이 되었음을 보여 준다. 또한 내기의 빚이 맹세로 바뀌었다고 생각하며, 열쇠를 돌리는 모습을 약속을 조이는 손길에 비유한다. 따라서 그 경쟁을 애정 어린 시선으로 감상하는 A가 정답이다. B는 짜증으로, C는 시계 관리에 대한 관심으로, D는 불공정에 대한 우려로 잘못 읽었다.

seed.relationship: a mother and a daughter planning a wedding
seed.topicSeed: a customs checkpoint in Tehran; a mother and a daughter planning a wedding while pretending nothing has changed

g.passage: When my mother and I stood in line at the customs checkpoint in Tehran, carrying a garment bag between us like a sleeping child, we talked only about the wedding. Which caterer, which flowers, whether Felix's family would expect a second reception. We did not talk about my father, who had always been the one to handle the officers and the forms, and who had died in March. My mother answered the officer's questions too quickly, then too slowly. I noticed she had brought his old fountain pen to sign the declaration. Nicolas, my fiancé's brother, waved from beyond the glass, and she waved back with exaggerated cheer. I found it hard to watch and harder to look away. I have since come to think that her pretending was a kind of bravery I did not yet possess. The officer stamped our papers without looking up.
g.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward her mother?
options: The narrator is embarrassed by her mother's nervousness and wishes she had traveled alone.
The narrator is tenderly respectful, seeing courage in her mother's forced cheer.
The narrator is frustrated that her mother refuses to plan the wedding in detail.
The narrator is amused by her mother's attempts to impress the officers at the checkpoint.
g.explanation: 화자는 어머니가 질문에 너무 빨리, 또 너무 느리게 답하고 남편의 만년필을 챙겨 온 모습을 세심하게 관찰한다. 또 과장된 쾌활함을 보기 힘들면서도 눈을 뗄 수 없었다고 말하고, 그 가장을 자신에게 아직 없던 용기로 해석한다. 따라서 어머니에게 애틋한 존중을 보이는 B가 정답이다. A는 당혹감과 혼자 여행하고 싶은 마음을, C와 D는 지문에 없는 좌절이나 즐거움을 내세운다.

seed.relationship: a retired sailor and his neighbor
seed.conflict: about a promise nobody remembers making
seed.topicSeed: a radio repair shop in Addis Ababa; a retired sailor and his neighbor about a promise nobody remembers making

g.passage: Static hissed from every shelf of Baraka's radio repair shop in Addis Ababa when Wanjiru brought in her late uncle's set. Baraka, a retired sailor, recognized it at once and said he had promised to fix it decades ago. Wanjiru remembered no such promise, and neither, she suspected, did he. Still, he worked on it for three evenings while she waited on a stool, and he told her stories of ports her uncle had never mentioned. On the fourth evening the radio played a song, faint but clear. Baraka seemed less pleased by the music than by the fact that she had stayed to hear it. Across the street, a vendor lowered the shutters on his stall of spices.
g.question: Which choice best states the main purpose of the passage?
options: To recount how a retired sailor repaired an old radio for a customer over several evenings
To describe the busy shops and vendors of a neighborhood in Addis Ababa at dusk
To show that kindness is always rewarded when people keep their promises to one another
To suggest that a forgotten promise serves mainly as a reason for two people to connect
g.explanation: Baraka는 Wanjiru도 자신도 기억하지 못하는 약속을 내세워 라디오를 고치며, 그동안 그녀에게 삼촌의 이야기를 들려준다. 또 그는 음악보다 그녀가 끝까지 남아 들어 주었다는 사실에 더 기뻐한다. 이 두 근거로 볼 때, 잊힌 약속은 두 사람이 이어지기 위한 구실이라는 D가 정답이다. A는 일화만 요약했고, B는 지문 소재를 쓰지만 목적이 다르며, C는 지나치게 일반적인 교훈이다.
